Supplementary Item 4 Continuous Flood Factor specifications

Imports the full continuous-score output, including coefficient and marginal-slope variants.

Source: docs/q2-robustness-FF-variable-forms.html#continuous-flood-factor-models.

Continuous Flood Factor Models

With property and year fixed effects, the continuous Flood Factor models do not estimate whether higher-score properties are generally cheaper than lower-score properties. That cross-sectional difference is absorbed by the property fixed effects. Instead, these models test whether post-release price trajectories differed systematically for properties with different Flood Factor scores.

The coefficient on env_flood_fs_factor:event is best interpreted as whether properties with higher Flood Factor scores had more negative post-release price changes than properties with lower Flood Factor scores, net of property and year fixed effects.

The following table identifies coefficients omitted from interpretation due to extremely large standard errors or lack of identification under the fixed-effects structure. Large standard errors typically indicate that a coefficient is not identified within the property fixed-effects framework because the underlying variable does not vary within parcels over time, or because certain interaction combinations contain extremely sparse observations.

Supplementary Item 5 Flood Factor score categories

Imports categorical-score estimates and associated plots/diagnostics from the ordinal model section. Units and contrast definitions follow the source.

Source: docs/q2-robustness-FF-variable-forms.html#ordinal-flood-factor-models.

Ordinal Flood Factor Models

The ordinal specifications estimate separate post-release effects for each Flood Factor score category. These models are useful for identifying whether the price response is concentrated among higher Flood Factor scores rather than changing linearly across the full scale.

The following table identifies coefficients omitted from interpretation due to extremely large standard errors or lack of identification under the fixed-effects structure. Large standard errors typically indicate that a coefficient is not identified within the property fixed-effects framework because the underlying variable does not vary within parcels over time, or because certain interaction combinations contain extremely sparse observations.

Supplementary Item 6 FEMA event studies

Current website sections retain plots, joint-test output and methodological notes for additions and removals.

Source: docs/q1-text-material.html#q1-added-event-study.

Additions: event study and pretrend tests

Properties added to the preliminary SFHA are compared with never-SFHA properties. Event time is relative to the preliminary map year; sales earlier than the preliminary date within that year are assigned to year -1. The endpoint bins pool years at or below -5 and at or above +5. Year -1 is the omitted reference period.

The plotted model uses logged sale price, property and year fixed effects, and standard errors clustered by 10-digit parcel. The coefficient table below the plot lists estimated pretreatment leads; the Wald test jointly tests the included leads -5 through -2 against zero relative to year -1. Rejection raises concerns about the specification or pre-event comparability. Non-rejection is not proof of parallel trends, especially when treated samples are small.

event_time_binned::-4:treated -0.5796238 0.0063581 -91.162598 0.0000000 -4
event_time_binned::-3:treated -0.2672640 0.0038471 -69.470805 0.0000000 -3
event_time_binned::-2:treated -0.0340017 0.0048248 -7.047211 0.0000000 -2 
Wald test, H0: joint nullity of event_time_binned::-5:treated, event_time_binned::-4:treated, event_time_binned::-3:treated and event_time_binned::-2:treated
 stat = 2,874.2, p-value < 2.2e-16, on 4 and 186,108 DoF, VCOV: Clustered (pin10).

Source: docs/q1-text-material.html#q1-removed-event-study.

Removals: event study and pretrend tests

Properties removed from the preliminary SFHA are compared with always-SFHA properties. The event-time bins, omitted period, fixed effects, and clustering follow the addition specification. The plot and joint lead test provide the removal-side diagnostics discussed in Appendix A; the appropriate comparison is within this design, rather than between its coefficient levels and those of the addition design.

[1] 2010 2025

This specification controls for common year effects but does not allow year effects to differ across North Cook, South Cook, and Chicago. The regional-control comparison below examines sensitivity to that restriction; the baseline specification alone does not establish whether regional differences explain its estimates.

term estimate std.error statistic p.value rel_time
event_time_binned::-5:treated -0.0272036 0.1429671 -0.1902788 0.8491055 -5
event_time_binned::-4:treated 0.1548045 0.0941084 1.6449593 0.1000987 -4
event_time_binned::-3:treated 0.0670327 0.0770443 0.8700546 0.3843506 -3
event_time_binned::-2:treated -0.0432119 0.1293224 -0.3341406 0.7383003 -2 
Wald test, H0: joint nullity of event_time_binned::-5:treated, event_time_binned::-4:treated, event_time_binned::-3:treated and event_time_binned::-2:treated
 stat = 1.16631, p-value = 0.323669, on 4 and 2,609 DoF, VCOV: Clustered (pin10).

Read the joint test as a test that the included pretreatment coefficients are zero relative to the omitted period. It is not a test that the coefficients equal one another, and a non-significant result does not prove parallel trends.

Distributional diagnostics and anticipation

The saved distributional diagnostics come from scripts/Q2_FloodFactor_didFF_test.R. That script uses the older data/processed/df_prep_buildings.rds input, applies its missing-data and parcel filters, averages observations within property-year, and assigns the treated group to 2020 for a property with a high Flood Factor score and an observed post-release sale. The last condition makes group assignment depend on observed sales as well as risk status. This historical construction must be reviewed before treating these outputs as a definitive check of the current main model.

The logged and unlogged saved objects both report p-values of 1. The displays below load those results without rerunning the exploratory script. They are not evidence that the current main-model sample passes every identifying assumption: failure to reject a distributional diagnostic does not prove mean parallel trends, absence of anticipation, or causal identification.


Logged sale price: historical Q2 diagnostic
Saved p-value: 1

What the anticipation checks can establish

The pre-event slope tests and the pre-2020 placebo sample address patterns before the recorded Flood Factor release. The existing placebo code defines its post period as years greater than 2017, so 2018-2019 are post-placebo and 2017 itself remains pre-placebo. A significant placebo interaction may reflect differential trends, other events, or anticipation; it does not distinguish among them. A non-significant result cannot rule out advance information or limited power. The assumed information date and sample construction must be considered alongside these diagnostics.

Supplementary Item 11 Flood Factor pre-release slope tests

The current section contains multiple specifications and regional tests, with source descriptions of outcome scale and controls. These are not all the same model as the printed Table XXIV.

Source: docs/q2-text-material.html#q2-pretrend-tests.

Pre-event slope tests

The first tables examine linear slope differences by SFHA and high Flood Factor status in sales before 2020, with parcel-clustered standard errors but no property fixed effects. Subsequent specifications use the recorded release date and include property/year fixed effects or split the comparison by triad, as labeled. These are different specifications and pre-period definitions. A non-significant interaction does not establish equivalence of trends; inspect its magnitude and precision as well as the p-value.

Supplementary Item 12 Flood Factor placebo and actual event

Retains all four current source columns so their risk, SFHA, time effects and sample distinctions remain visible. The source placebo code uses years greater than 2017; 2017 itself is pre-placebo.

Source: docs/q2-text-material.html#q2-placebo-tests.

Placebo analysis: existing 2017 cutoff

Dissertation Appendix B, Table XXV (p. 106), prints 659,942 observations for the actual event. We treat that count as a reporting error. The corresponding model with SFHA interactions uses 666,566 observations on the saved dissertation data, consistent with the sample size in the main text. Its high Flood Factor × post coefficient rounds to the printed −0.103.

Use each model’s actual estimation sample. The search for the origin of 659,942 is closed. If a future dissertation model independently yields exactly 659,942 estimation observations, flag it as a possible source of the printed count and record its specification and input file. A count match alone leaves the provenance uncertain.

The first two models restrict sales to 2019 or earlier and define post-placebo as sale_year > 2017: 2018-2019 versus earlier years. The next two show actual-release specifications using the broader prepared sample. Their time windows and some fixed effects differ, so they are reference models rather than an exact one-variable timing substitution. This makes the existing implementation explicit without silently changing the dissertation’s placebo design.

Regional controls and conditional parallel trends

Appendix A considers whether regional housing-market differences affect the Q1 comparisons. The specifications below adapt the existing triad-by-year event studies in q1_assumption_tests.qmd to the same addition and removal samples used above. They replace common year effects with sale_year^Triad while retaining property fixed effects and parcel-clustered standard errors. These are region-by-year fixed effects, not separate linear trend slopes.

The comparisons use a common complete-case sample for each treatment direction, so differences between the two specifications are not caused by missing triad identifiers. The joint tests concern the included pretreatment coefficients relative to year -1; failure to reject does not establish the unobserved post-treatment counterfactual. These tables are newly assembled from the existing specifications, not a verified reproduction of a numbered dissertation table.

Outcome transformations

Appendix A (printed pages 95-97) discusses sale price in levels, logarithms, inverse price, and inverse hyperbolic sine. The plots below assemble all four transformations for the Q1 event-study samples. They use the same observations across transformations: finite, strictly positive prices in the pretreatment period, with addition and removal comparisons shown separately. The last two plots are supporting variations, not estimates of a new treatment effect.

Points are means of transformed sale prices by calendar year and treatment group, not transformations of the group mean. The panels use separate vertical scales. A year can pool observations from different preliminary-map cohorts, and the mix of sold properties can change over time; these descriptive plots therefore supplement the event studies rather than proving parallel trends. Inverse price is decreasing in price, so its direction must be interpreted accordingly. This newly assembled comparison is not an exact reconstruction of dissertation Figures 15-16.

Source: docs/q1-text-material.html#q1-distributional-tests.

Saved distributional parallel-trends diagnostics

Appendix A (printed pages 98-99) reports distributional diagnostics associated with Roth and Sant’Anna’s functional-form analysis. Existing results were located in scripts/Q1_SFHA_DiD_test.R and its saved didFF objects. The cells below display those saved results without re-estimating them or running the exploratory script.

The unlogged 2014/2022 object has a saved p-value of 0.99778, consistent with the rounded 0.998 in the dissertation. A second unlogged object has p-value 1. The saved logged-price object has p-value 0. These are different historical specifications; they should not be presented as uniformly supporting the same conclusion. The script overwrites the logged-price output during its later exploratory specification, so it is not a clean same-sample levels-versus-logs comparison. A large p-value is a failure to reject the diagnostic’s null, not proof of parallel trends or of the causal interpretation.

Saved object Code provenance and interpretation
didFF_Q1_model_notlogged.rds Uses the older parcel dataset df_prep_land_updated_final.rds, retains 2014 and 2022 sales, averages within property-year, and assigns the transition group to 2022. Outcome: sale price.
didFF_Q1_model_out.rds Last written by the later logged-price specification, which assigns group 2021 using transition status and sale date relative to the preliminary date. This assignment can vary within property.
didFF_model_Q1_out2.rds Later unlogged-price specification with the same sale-date-dependent group construction. It is distinct from the 2014/2022 comparison.

The latter two grouping constructions require methodological review before being used as confirmatory evidence. The saved objects do not establish that these samples match the current building-based Q1 models. The historical output is shown here to make the dissertation’s diagnostic evidence traceable, including the result that differs from its summary.

---
title: "Supporting items for NTA Conference Paper"
date: 2026-11-12
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  error: false
  freeze: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(xml2)
root <- normalizePath(Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR", unset = ".."))
assets <- file.path(root, "NTA_2026/website_source_assets")
dir.create(assets, showWarnings = FALSE)
provenance <- data.frame(file=character(), selector=character(), md5=character())
source_path <- function(file) {
 # Quarto stages website pages in the project root before publishing to docs.
 staged <- file.path(root, sub("^docs/", "", file))
 if (startsWith(file, "docs/") && file.exists(staged)) return(staged)
 file.path(root, file)
}
read_source <- function(file) {
 p <- source_path(file)
 if (!file.exists(p)) stop("Missing rendered source: ", p)
 read_html(p)
}
record <- function(file, selector) {
 provenance <<- rbind(provenance, data.frame(file=file,selector=selector,md5=unname(tools::md5sum(source_path(file)))))
}
emit <- function(node, file) {
 # Drop code and interactive controls; preserve results and source notes.
 xml_remove(xml_find_all(node, ".//script|.//style|.//details|.//*[contains(@class,'cell-code')]|.//*[contains(@class,'sourceCode')]|.//*[contains(@class,'anchorjs')]|.//*[contains(@class,'cell-output-error')]|.//button"))
 for (img in xml_find_all(node, ".//img")) {
  src <- xml_attr(img,"src")
  if (grepl("^data:",src)) next
  p <- file.path(dirname(source_path(file)),URLdecode(src))
  if (!file.exists(p)) stop("Missing source image: ",p)
  name <- paste0(substr(unname(tools::md5sum(p)),1,12),"_",basename(p))
  file.copy(p,file.path(assets,name),overwrite=TRUE)
  xml_set_attr(img,"src",paste0("website_source_assets/",name))
 }
 # Static tables and plots do not require the source page's tabset JavaScript.
 for (x in xml_find_all(node,".//*[@class]")) {
  cls <- xml_attr(x,"class")
  if (grepl("tab-pane",cls)) xml_set_attr(x,"class","imported-panel")
 }
 cat('\n````{=html}\n<div class="imported-output">', as.character(node),
     '</div>\n````\n\n', sep = "")
}
import_section <- function(file,id,tables=NULL) {
 doc <- read_source(file);node <- xml_find_first(doc,paste0("//*[@id='",id,"']"))
 if (inherits(node,"xml_missing")) stop("Missing source anchor: ",file,"#",id)
 record(file,id)
 cat("\nSource: `",file,"#",id,"`.\n\n",sep="")
 if (is.null(tables)) {
  emit(node,file)
 } else {
  nodes <- xml_find_all(node,".//table")
  if (max(tables)>length(nodes)) stop("Requested source table is missing: ",id)
  for (i in tables) emit(nodes[[i]],file)
 }
}
import_plots <- function(file,indices) {
 doc <- read_source(file);nodes <- xml_find_all(doc,"//main//img")
 if (max(indices)>length(nodes)) stop("Source plot index is missing")
 record(file,paste0("main images ",paste(indices,collapse=",")))
 for(i in indices) {
  wrapper <- read_html(paste0('<div><p>Source plot: ',htmltools::htmlEscape(xml_attr(nodes[[i]],'src')),'</p>',as.character(nodes[[i]]),'</div>'))
  emit(xml_find_first(wrapper,"//body/div"),file)
 }
}
```
